Запрос 1. Результаты литературного поиска

Необходимо подобрать альтернативу стандартному фенольному антиоксиданту для моторного масла, но с улучшенной термостойкостью. Нужна оценка возможности синтеза на основе доступных алкилфенолов, чтобы получить лабораторный образец массой не менее 2 граммов, с итоговой чистота не ниже 85%, подтверждённая хроматографией. Параметр окислительной активности в реальном масле не известен, но важно предложить методику для её быстрой оценки на начальном этапе. Желательно использовать доступное сырье и избегать длительных сроков поставки.

1Trends in Structure and Ethylene Polymerization Reactivity of Transition-Metal Permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) Complexes
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 18%retrieval 93%

This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. Methodology involved synthesizing complexes, exchanging chloride ligands with various groups (halides, alkyls, etc.), and characterizing solid-state structures. Results showed that PHENI* catalysts, particularly titanium-based, exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for ethylene polymerization when heterogenized on sMAO. The study found that catalyst structure affects activity and ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) formation, offering insights into ion pairing and ligand geometry. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

Keywords/terms: ansa, PHENI*, PHENICS, permethylindenyl, Ethylene Polymerization, sMAO, UHMWPE, Ti, Zr, Hf.

2Crystal structure, spectroscopy, DFT, and thermal studies of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones as potential anticancer agents
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 18%retrieval 91%

This 2024 study investigates the synthesis, characterization, and potential anticancer activity of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones. The objective was to explore the physicochemical and biological properties of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones as potential anticancer agents, addressing gaps in existing knowledge. The methodology involved a microwave-assisted multicomponent approach for efficient synthesis, single-crystal XRD analysis for crystal structure determination, DFT calculations to understand electronic structures, spectroscopic techniques (FT-IR, UV-Vis, NMR) for structure confirmation, thermal analysis (DSC, TGA) for thermal stability assessment, and in vitro anticancer activity evaluation against 60 human cancer cell lines. Compounds 4a and 4c exhibited the highest anticancer activity against non-small-cell lung (HOP-92) and breast cancer (MCF7) cell lines. The work is novel because it provides a comprehensive study of these compounds, including crystal structure, DFT analysis, and anticancer activity which was not done before.

3Bimetallic Zirconium Amine Bis(phenolate) Polymerization Catalysts: Enhanced Activity and Tacticity Control for Polyolefin Synthesis
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 15%retrieval 88%
Keywords/terms: bimetallic catalysts, zirconium, amine bis(phenolate), polymerization, polyolefin, tacticity control, isotacticity, 1-hexene, propylene.

The study, published in 2014, focuses on the design and synthesis of bimetallic zirconium amine bis(phenolate) precatalysts for polyolefin synthesis. The objective was to enhance activity and control tacticity in propylene and 1-hexene polymerization. The methodology involved synthesizing bimetallic precatalysts with rigid terphenyl backbones and evaluating their performance against monometallic analogues. The primary findings reveal that the bimetallic precatalysts demonstrated significantly higher isotacticity (up to 79% mmmm) and activity (up to 124 kg of poly(1-hexene) (mmol of Zr)-1 h-1) compared to monometallic counterparts. The stereocontrol is attributed to bimetallic mechanisms involving steric interactions. This work distinguishes itself by effectively utilizing bimetallic catalysts to achieve enhanced activity and stereocontrol in olefin polymerization.

4Extraction of phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil by deep eutectic solvent (DES)
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 9%retrieval 83%
Keywords/terms: Deep eutectic solvents, Extraction, Phenolic compounds, Oleacein, Oleocanthal, Virgin olive oil. The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. Results indicated that DESs, particularly ChCl/xylitol and ChCl/1,2-propanediol, showed good solubility for phenolic compounds. Specifically, the study found an increase in extraction yields of oleacein and oleocanthal by 20–33% and 67.9–68.3%, respectively, compared to conventional methods. This work distinguishes itself by being the first to extract phenolic compounds from VOO using DESs, proposing a more efficient, safer, sustainable, and cost-effective alternative to methanol.

5Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents as a New Extraction Media for Phenolic Metabolites in Carthamus tinctorius L.
Chemical EngineeringPhysical Sciencesrerank 6%retrieval 95%
Keywords/terms: Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents (NADES), Phenolic compounds, Carthamus tinctorius L., Extraction, HPLC, PCA. The study, published in 2013, investigates the use of Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents (NADES) as novel extraction media for phenolic compounds from safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.). The objective was to assess NADES' efficiency in extracting compounds of varying polarity, optimize extraction parameters, and recover the extracted compounds. The methodology involved using different NADES, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) for analysis, and principal component analysis (PCA). Results indicated that NADES, particularly lactic acid-glucose, proline-malic acid, and sucrose-choline chloride, exhibited superior or comparable extraction efficiency compared to conventional solvents like ethanol. NADES were also found to be effective for the recovery of the extracted phenolic compounds. The study highlights the potential of NADES as green solvents for the extraction of bioactive compounds, differing from previous studies by focusing on the use of natural compounds for the solvents and their application for extraction of phenolic compounds from plant material.

6Photoactivated Artificial Molecular Motors
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 5%retrieval 93%
Keywords/terms: molecular machines, photochemistry, autonomous operation, directional motion, dissipative systems, nanoratchets. Title: Photoactivated Artificial Molecular Motors. Year: 2023. Objective: The review article discusses the design, operation, and potential of light-driven artificial molecular motors, highlighting their applications in energy storage and bionanotechnology. Methodology: The review focuses on recent examples of light-driven artificial molecular motors, assessing design criteria, operation, and technological potential. The study examines rotary motors based on covalent molecular structures with examples of overcrowded alkenes and imines. Additionally, the review analyzes linear motors based on supramolecular complexes, particularly rotaxane-like architectures. Results: The review presents an overview of photoactivated artificial molecular motors, categorizing them into covalent rotary motors and supramolecular linear motors. It discusses the working principles, operation cycles, molecular designs, and prospective applications. The study also covers examples where molecular motors transmit controlled motion and control molecular topology. Furthermore, the article highlights the use of these motors in creating complex molecular structures and controlling macroscopic properties, such as hydrogels, as well as their potential applications in cell membrane transport and materials science. The article "Exploring the Potential of PEG-Based Deep Eutectic Solvents as a Sustainable Alternative for Extraction of Biological Macromolecules Bovine Serum Hemoglobin" (2025) investigates the use of PEG-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as a sustainable alternative for extracting bovine serum hemoglobin (BHb). The study prepared and characterized four novel PEG-based DESs, evaluating their physicochemical properties. The methodology involved testing the DESs for the selective extraction of BHb, with DES-4 achieving the highest extraction efficiency of 88%. Spectroscopic techniques were employed to investigate extraction mechanisms and protein interactions. Results indicated successful extraction and protein stability, with DES-4 (PEG-600) showing the most promising results. The study highlights the potential of PEG-based DESs as environmentally friendly substitutes for conventional separation techniques, offering an efficient and sustainable platform for protein extraction.

Keywords/terms: Zirconocene catalysis, Carbomagnesation, Cyclic ethers, Enantioselectivity, Regioselectivity, Diastereoselectivity.

The 1994 article "Enantio-, Diastereo-, and Regioselective Zirconium-Catalyzed Carbomagnesation of Cyclic Ethers with Higher Alkyls of Magnesium. Utility in Synthesis and Mechanistic Implications" investigates the zirconium-catalyzed carbomagnesation of cyclic ethers using higher alkyls of magnesium. The objective was to explore the enantioselective C-C bond formation. The methodology involved reacting cyclic ethers with n-PrMgCl and n-BuMgCl in the presence of a chiral zirconocene catalyst, followed by analysis of the products. The results showed that the reaction afforded homoallylic and bishomoallylic alcohols with high enantioselectivity, regiocontrol, and, when n-BuMgCl was used, diastereochemical control. Novel aspects included the enhanced regioselectivity at elevated temperatures and the unusual modes of preference for the regioselectivity in p-hydride abstraction. The study also elucidated mechanistic insights such as the role of syn and anti isomers of zirconocene-alkene complexes and the factors influencing temperature-dependent selectivity.

Objective: To synthesize citric acid-functionalized rhodium-platinum nanoparticles (CA-RhPt NPs) as peroxidase mimics and apply them for sensitive cholesterol detection. BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The objective is to find improved conditions for C-C bond formation, specifically in the context of α,β-unsaturated aldehydes, where conventional methods face limitations. The novelty lies in the use of LiI and its applicability to unsaturated aldehydes, improving upon the limitations of previous base-catalyzed processes and phase-transfer catalysis.

Methodology: The study employed an electrochemical paired electrolysis approach using alcohol-derived carbazates and nitrobenzene. Mechanistic studies included radical trapping experiments, investigation of reaction intermediates, and cyclic voltammetry. Results: A general electrochemical paired electrolysis method was developed for synthesizing primary, secondary, and tertiary amines from functionalized alcohols, including those with α-CF3, α-CF2H, and benzyl substituents. The findings highlight the successful harnessing of stabilized and activated radicals for further derivatization which differed from prior studies.

BODY: Objective: To develop a microfluidic synthesis method for oligohexamethylene guanidine bihydrocarbonate (OHMG-BHC) in a flow-type reactor, evaluate its efficiency compared to classical bulk synthesis, and assess the purity of the resulting products. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. The structural integrity and purity of the products were analyzed using 13C NMR spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Results: 13C NMR analysis revealed that the microfluidic method successfully yielded a branched oligomeric structure with fewer unidentifiable impurities compared to bulk synthesis. HPLC analysis showed that the microfluidic approach resulted in a 1.5-fold lower concentration of unreacted initial monomers (hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate). Novelty: This study demonstrates the advantages of utilizing continuous-flow microfluidic hardware over traditional bulk reactors to streamline the synthesis of OHMG derivatives while significantly enhancing chemical purity and reaction completeness.

This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The objective was to develop a sensitive and selective method for detecting antioxidants using a MnO2/Graphene Quantum Dot (GQD) composite with oxidase-like activity. BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

KEYWORDS: [microfluidic conditions, acid-mediated reactions, natural products synthesis, oligosaccharides, pristane, glycosylation, reductive opening, benzylidene acetal, dehydration, micromixing, continuous flow microreactor, N-glycans, stereoselective synthesis]

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

Utilizing a 2-D PDMS microfluidic device with a central fracture flanked by high- and low-permeability zones, pre-generated foam (using alpha olefin sulfonate and lauryl betaine surfactants) was injected to displace paraffin oil. The objective was to observe multi-phase fluid transport and pore-level displacement phenomena compared against control methods like water flooding and water-alternating-gas (WAG) injection. Results indicate that foam significantly improves sweep efficiency and oil recovery across all permeability zones, particularly in the difficult-to-sweep low-permeability matrix, by increasing flow resistance and redirecting pressure gradients. Furthermore, the study reveals that foam phase-separates in heterogeneous media: the liquid surfactant phase readily invades smaller pores at lower capillary entry pressures, while gas bubbles remain trapped in higher permeability channels, demonstrating that foam cannot be treated as a homogeneous dispersion. BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

KEYWORDS: microfluidic reactor, hydroxymethyl phosphonates, continuous synthesis, phosphite esters, formaldehyde, flow chemistry, high yield, high purity, acid number, green chemistry, optimization, dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate, diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate, mass transfer, heat transfer.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

The objective was to fabricate uniform oil-core/polymer-shell microcapsules with precisely controlled sizes and ultra-thin shells. Monodisperse nanoliter-sized Janus droplets comprising an acrylate monomer (1,6-hexanediol diacrylate) and silicone oil were generated in an aqueous polyvinyl alcohol continuous phase. Due to interfacial energy minimization, these droplets spontaneously evolved from a Janus geometry to a core-shell structure. Subsequent off-chip photo- and thermally induced polymerization solidified the monomer shells. By systematically varying the flow rate ratios and increasing the photo- or thermal initiator concentrations, the authors successfully fabricated microcapsules with ultra-thin shells down to 800 nm thickness. Results indicate that photopolymerization yields smooth surface morphologies, whereas thermally induced polymerization creates porous surfaces due to nitrogen gas generation from initiator decomposition. This methodology offers a robust, one-step-like templating approach for producing functionalized microcapsules suitable for drug delivery, cosmetics, and self-healing materials. The methodology involves utilizing continuous-flow, droplet-based, and digital microfluidic platforms to control reactant mixing, supersaturation, and reaction-diffusion processes. BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This paper investigates the formation of poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) microparticles and capsules via the selective extraction of aqueous polymer solution droplets generated using microfluidics and immersed in a non-solvent bath. The objective is to quantify the role of polymer molecular mass, degree of hydrolysis, and initial concentration on particle formation, dimensions, internal microstructure, and extraction timescales. Using a flow-focusing geometry, monodisperse droplets were produced in a hexadecane carrier phase and extracted into ethyl acetate. A descriptive model was applied to parameterize droplet shrinkage and extraction kinetics. Results demonstrate that initial polymer concentration is the primary factor determining final particle size and extraction timescales, while polymer molecular mass and hydrolysis play secondary roles, provided concentrations are above the overlap concentration (c*). For concentrations well below c*, ultrathin-walled capsules (100s of nm) were formed, which crumpled or buckled upon extraction. Furthermore, anisotropic extraction near impermeable surfaces yielded large cavities without disrupting internal porosity. The novelty lies in establishing comprehensive design criteria for PVA particles and capsules, linking thermodynamic and hydrodynamic factors to final morphology.

Keywords/terms: nanozyme, optical sensor, oxidase-mimetic activity, manganese dioxide, graphene quantum dots, food analysis.

This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The objective was to develop a sensitive and selective method for detecting antioxidants using a MnO2/Graphene Quantum Dot (GQD) composite with oxidase-like activity. The methodology involved synthesizing the composite via a hydrothermal method and using it as a nanozyme to catalyze the oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB), quantified by color changes. The results showed the developed assay achieved high selectivity and sensitivity for gallic acid, tannic acid, and ascorbic acid, with detection limits of 0.07, 0.28, and 0.69 μmol L−1, respectively. The sensor accurately measured and discriminated antioxidants in real food samples, demonstrating its potential for rapid food analysis. This work distinguishes itself by its use of an oxidase-like nanozyme, which eliminates the need for hydrogen peroxide, providing a simpler and more stable sensing system compared to peroxidase-mimicking nanozymes.

Methodology: A 3D-printed PDMS microfluidic chip was integrated with a ratiometric fluorescence nanoprobe composed of carbon dots embedded in an Eu3+-based metal-organic framework (EuMOF/CDs). Spiked milk and serum samples achieved satisfactory recoveries ranging from 85% to 104.6%. Novelty: The work presents a fully integrated, dual-mode, 3D-printed microfluidic chip combined with a smartphone readout for DPA detection, offering dual signal validation, self-calibration, and robust anti-interference capabilities for field-ready analytical screening. This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. Methodology involved synthesizing complexes, exchanging chloride ligands with various groups (halides, alkyls, etc.), and characterizing solid-state structures. Results showed that PHENI* catalysts, particularly titanium-based, exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for ethylene polymerization when heterogenized on sMAO. The study found that catalyst structure affects activity and ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) formation, offering insights into ion pairing and ligand geometry. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

The article, published in 2018, reports on the asymmetric Michael addition reactions catalyzed by iron N-heterocyclic carbene (FeNHC) complexes. The objective was to study the Michael addition reactions of cyclic b-oxo ester and a-methyl cyano ester substrates with activated olefins using FeNHC complexes. The methodology involved synthesizing {Cp[1-benzyl-3-alkyl-benzimidazol-2-ylidene]Fe(CO)2}I complexes, where alkyl = i-Pr and Et, and employing them as catalysts in the presence of L-proline under ambient conditions. The results showed that the cyclic b-oxo ester substrates yielded up to 68% with 18% enantioselectivities, while the a-methyl cyano ester substrates gave up to 82% yields with 8% enantioselectivities. The study's novelty lies in the use of FeNHC complexes in the asymmetric Michael addition, which has not been extensively explored, and the mechanism was proposed based on mass spectrometry results.

The objective was to understand how the ancillary ligand influences the catalytic performance in ethylene polymerization. Various complexes, including [Cp*Ti(2-R-PhO)nCl3n], were prepared and characterized. DFT calculations supported the experimental findings, suggesting [Cp*Ti(2-Ph-PhO)MeCl] as the active species. Furthermore, homopolymerization of ethylene was carried out with methylated complexes, and the activity was correlated with the generation of active sites. Objective: To develop a general and efficient method for the deoxygenative amination of activated alcohols, particularly those with challenging substituents like trifluoromethyl groups. Methodology: The study employed an electrochemical paired electrolysis approach using alcohol-derived carbazates and nitrobenzene. Various primary, secondary, and tertiary alkylamines were synthesized. Optimization of reaction conditions was performed to maximize yields. Mechanistic studies included radical trapping experiments, investigation of reaction intermediates, and cyclic voltammetry. Results: A general electrochemical paired electrolysis method was developed for synthesizing primary, secondary, and tertiary amines from functionalized alcohols, including those with α-CF3, α-CF2H, and benzyl substituents. The method utilized carbazates and nitroarenes. The practicality of the method was demonstrated using electrochemical continuous flow technique, and a plausible reaction mechanism was proposed, with yields ranging from 38-74%. The findings highlight the successful harnessing of stabilized and activated radicals for further derivatization which differed from prior studies.

Methodology involved controlling injection rates (0.001 to 0.01 dimensionless volumetric injection rates) and measuring residence time distributions (RTDs) using an inline UV-vis setup with a sodium benzoate tracer. Results indicate that increasing dispersant concentration transitions the system from a stable slug flow to a stochastic bubbly flow regime, with critical dimensionless mass ratios estimated between 2.6×10^-3 and 7.7×10^-3 depending on kerosene content. The novelty lies in utilizing microfluidics combined with classical chemical engineering reactor design principles to identify critical dispersant mass thresholds that maximize oil surface-to-volume ratios for enhanced bacterial consumption while reducing excess chemical usage in calm-sea marine environments.

BODY: Objective: To develop a sensitive, reproducible, and continuous surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) detection platform for trace molecules in solution, addressing limitations in uniformity and molecular adsorption. Methodology: Plasmonic core-satellite nanostructures were synthesized by immobilizing high-density gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) onto 0.54-um silica beads, followed by the growth of a fine-tuned silver (Ag) shell to optimize nanogaps and electromagnetic hot spots. Capping agents (citrate) were displaced using alkali halides (specifically potassium bromide, KBr) to reduce background signals and enhance molecular adsorption. These nanostructures were then accumulated onto a cellulose acetate membrane filter integrated within a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic device, allowing sample solutions to continuously flow through the substrate. Results: The integrated microfluidic SERS device achieved continuous detection of malachite green (MG) down to a limit of detection of 500 fM, and successfully demonstrated sequential monitoring of varying fluid compositions (such as NaSCN and MG). Novelty: The combination of a high-density core-satellite plasmonic substrate with a flow-through membrane-integrated microfluidic architecture significantly amplifies molecular adsorption and ensures uniform SERS signals, outperforming traditional static droplet-drying methods.

BODY: This study investigates the control over the crystal structure and stability of a model low molecular weight organic compound, succinic acid, using a microfluidic surface acoustic wave (SAW)-based spray-drying technique. The primary objective was to overcome the limitations of conventional bulk processing and explore how processing conditions, particularly supersaturation rates driven by initial solute concentration and solvent vapor pressure, influence polymorph selection and shelf-life stability. Solutions of succinic acid in ethanol, acetone, or deionized water were atomized into microscale droplets using a SAW device, leading to rapid evaporation within milliseconds. Results demonstrate that high supersaturation rates—achieved via low initial solute concentrations (e.g., 10 mM) or solvents with high vapor pressures—kinetically favor the formation and stabilization of the metastable alpha phase of succinic acid, preventing immediate transformation into the stable beta phase. Conversely, lower supersaturation rates promote premature precipitation and the inclusion of stable nuclei, accelerating phase transformation during storage. Furthermore, the incorporation of additives such as vanillin promotes phase separation and acts as heterogeneous nucleation sites, whereas maltol enhances the stability of the metastable phase. The novelty lies in utilizing high-throughput, microfluidic SAW-based spray drying to precisely manipulate the polymorphism and storage stability of low molecular weight organic carriers without costly additives.

BODY: This study investigates the control over the crystal structure and stability of a model low molecular weight organic compound, succinic acid, using a microfluidic surface acoustic wave (SAW)-based spray-drying technique. The primary objective was to overcome the limitations of conventional bulk processing and explore how processing conditions, particularly supersaturation rates driven by initial solute concentration and solvent vapor pressure, influence polymorph selection and shelf-life stability. Solutions of succinic acid in ethanol, acetone, or deionized water were atomized into microscale droplets using a SAW device, leading to rapid evaporation within milliseconds. Results demonstrate that high supersaturation rates—achieved via low initial solute concentrations (e.g., 10 mM) or solvents with high vapor pressures—kinetically favor the formation and stabilization of the metastable alpha phase of succinic acid, preventing immediate transformation into the stable beta phase. Conversely, lower supersaturation rates promote premature precipitation and the inclusion of stable nuclei, accelerating phase transformation during storage. Furthermore, the incorporation of additives such as vanillin promotes phase separation and acts as heterogeneous nucleation sites, whereas maltol enhances the stability of the metastable phase. The novelty lies in utilizing high-throughput, microfluidic SAW-based spray drying to precisely manipulate the polymorphism and storage stability of low molecular weight organic carriers without costly additives.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

This 2024 study investigates the synthesis, characterization, and potential anticancer activity of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones. The objective was to explore the physicochemical and biological properties of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones as potential anticancer agents, addressing gaps in existing knowledge. The methodology involved a microwave-assisted multicomponent approach for efficient synthesis, single-crystal XRD analysis for crystal structure determination, DFT calculations to understand electronic structures, spectroscopic techniques (FT-IR, UV-Vis, NMR) for structure confirmation, thermal analysis (DSC, TGA) for thermal stability assessment, and in vitro anticancer activity evaluation against 60 human cancer cell lines. Compounds 4a and 4c exhibited the highest anticancer activity against non-small-cell lung (HOP-92) and breast cancer (MCF7) cell lines. BODY: This paper presents a novel one-step on-chip microfluidic approach for synthesizing hybrid hydrogel capsules using an aqueous two-phase system (ATPS) and a pneumatic valve-integrated device. The objective is to provide a green, oil-free alternative to traditional water-in-oil emulsion systems for biomedical applications, specifically overcoming the challenge of ultralow interfacial tension in water-in-water (w/w) emulsions. The methodology involves utilizing sodium alginate (SA) dissolved in a dextran (DEX) core phase, polyethylene glycol (PEG) as the middle phase, and chitosan dissolved in PEG as the shell phase. A pneumatic valve applies periodic mechanical pressure to facilitate stable, monodisperse droplet generation at the first flow-focusing junction. Subsequently, interfacial complexation via electrostatic interactions between oppositely charged polyelectrolytes (SA and chitosan) forms a robust solid shell. Results demonstrate that tuning the core and middle phase flow rates, alongside valve pressure, precisely controls droplet and capsule size. The capsules successfully encapsulated Fe2O3 magnetic particles while maintaining structural integrity and narrow size distribution (CV of 5.39%). The novelty lies in integrating a pneumatic valve with a settling collection method in an ATPS microfluidic device, enabling scalable, surfactant-free production of stable hydrogel capsules suitable for targeted drug delivery and cell encapsulation. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

This 2024 study investigates the synthesis, characterization, and potential anticancer activity of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones. The objective was to explore the physicochemical and biological properties of 3-cyano-2(1H)-pyridones as potential anticancer agents, addressing gaps in existing knowledge. The methodology involved a microwave-assisted multicomponent approach for efficient synthesis, single-crystal XRD analysis for crystal structure determination, DFT calculations to understand electronic structures, spectroscopic techniques (FT-IR, UV-Vis, NMR) for structure confirmation, thermal analysis (DSC, TGA) for thermal stability assessment, and in vitro anticancer activity evaluation against 60 human cancer cell lines. Compounds 4a and 4c exhibited the highest anticancer activity against non-small-cell lung (HOP-92) and breast cancer (MCF7) cell lines. The methodology involves formulating four micellar nanocarriers using FDA-approved surfactants (Cremophor EL and Tween 80) and oil phases (ethyl oleate and Miglyol 840) containing the TF-UC pair platinum(II) octaethylporphyrin and 9,10-diphenylanthracene. The results demonstrate that nanocarriers incorporating an oxygen-scavenging oil phase (ethyl oleate) significantly improve oxygen tolerability, retaining approximately 80% of their TF-UC emission at the mean tumor oxygen level (1.4%), compared to 40% for non-scavenging formulations. The novelty lies in the application of oxygen-depleting microfluidic chips for screening nanocarrier performance across physiological oxygen gradients, providing a more realistic evaluation method for biomedical and life science applications. BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

10Acid-mediated reactions under microfluidic conditions: A new strategy for practical synthesis of biofunctional natural products

KEYWORDS: [microfluidic conditions, acid-mediated reactions, natural products synthesis, oligosaccharides, pristane, glycosylation, reductive opening, benzylidene acetal, dehydration, micromixing, continuous flow microreactor, N-glycans, stereoselective synthesis]

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: Objective: To develop a microfluidic synthesis method for oligohexamethylene guanidine bihydrocarbonate (OHMG-BHC) in a flow-type reactor, evaluate its efficiency compared to classical bulk synthesis, and assess the purity of the resulting products. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. The structural integrity and purity of the products were analyzed using 13C NMR spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Results: 13C NMR analysis revealed that the microfluidic method successfully yielded a branched oligomeric structure with fewer unidentifiable impurities compared to bulk synthesis. HPLC analysis showed that the microfluidic approach resulted in a 1.5-fold lower concentration of unreacted initial monomers (hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate). Novelty: This study demonstrates the advantages of utilizing continuous-flow microfluidic hardware over traditional bulk reactors to streamline the synthesis of OHMG derivatives while significantly enhancing chemical purity and reaction completeness.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This mini-review introduces microfluidic plasma as a novel process intensification strategy that integrates microfluidic systems with plasma technology, leveraging their synergistic advantages for chemistry and chemical engineering. The objective is to highlight how miniaturized plasma configurations can overcome traditional mass and heat transfer limitations while operating under mild conditions (low temperature, atmospheric pressure, and often without catalysts). The methodology categorizes microfluidic plasmas into three primary configurations based on reactor design: chip-based, tubular-based, and jet-based microfluidic plasmas. The results demonstrate the broad utility and high efficiency of these systems across diverse applications, including the continuous synthesis of ligand-free gold nanoparticles and carbon dots, enhanced chemical synthesis (such as cyclohexane amination and hydrogen peroxide production), water treatment (organic pollutant degradation and biofilm removal), and surface/biomedical modifications. The novelty lies in combining small-scale fluid manipulation physics with strong nonequilibrium plasma chemistry to achieve high reaction rates, product purity, and process flexibility that cannot be attained by conventional technologies alone. BODY: This review article explores the recent advancements and applications of microfluidic paper-based analytical extraction devices (µPAEDs) as a cost-effective, portable, and decentralized solution for detecting biomarkers, chemical contaminants, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Conventional extraction methods coupled with high-end chromatography (such as LC-MS/MS and GC-MS/MS) are often expensive, slow, require centralized facilities, and use environmentally harmful reagents. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed all-in-one µPAEDs that integrate sample extraction and detection onto a single paper-based platform. The article highlights the classification and detection of various analytes across diverse sample types—including blood, urine, saliva, sweat, interstitial fluid, food, water, and breath. Furthermore, it details the integration of technologies like molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs), ion-imprinted polymers (IIPs), digital image colorimetry (DIC), and electrochemical sensing. The novelty of this review lies in its comprehensive compilation of recent innovations in µPAEDs, emphasizing both invasive and non-invasive testing (such as VOC breath analysis) and outlining future perspectives toward smart, wearable diagnostic tools.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. Methodology involved synthesizing complexes, exchanging chloride ligands with various groups (halides, alkyls, etc.), and characterizing solid-state structures. Results showed that PHENI* catalysts, particularly titanium-based, exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for ethylene polymerization when heterogenized on sMAO. The study found that catalyst structure affects activity and ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) formation, offering insights into ion pairing and ligand geometry. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

The methodology involves utilizing continuous-flow, droplet-based, and digital microfluidic platforms to control reactant mixing, supersaturation, and reaction-diffusion processes. The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. Results indicated that DESs, particularly ChCl/xylitol and ChCl/1,2-propanediol, showed good solubility for phenolic compounds. Specifically, the study found an increase in extraction yields of oleacein and oleocanthal by 20–33% and 67.9–68.3%, respectively, compared to conventional methods. This work distinguishes itself by being the first to extract phenolic compounds from VOO using DESs, proposing a more efficient, safer, sustainable, and cost-effective alternative to methanol.

The study, published in 2013, investigates the use of Natural Deep Eutectic Solvents (NADES) as novel extraction media for phenolic compounds from safflower (Carthamus tinctorius L.). The objective was to assess NADES' efficiency in extracting compounds of varying polarity, optimize extraction parameters, and recover the extracted compounds. The methodology involved using different NADES, high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) for analysis, and principal component analysis (PCA). Results indicated that NADES, particularly lactic acid-glucose, proline-malic acid, and sucrose-choline chloride, exhibited superior or comparable extraction efficiency compared to conventional solvents like ethanol. NADES were also found to be effective for the recovery of the extracted phenolic compounds. The study highlights the potential of NADES as green solvents for the extraction of bioactive compounds, differing from previous studies by focusing on the use of natural compounds for the solvents and their application for extraction of phenolic compounds from plant material.

9A CONTINUOUS SYNTHESIS METHOD OF HYDROXYLMETHYL PHOSPHONATES USING THE MICROFLUIDIC REACTOR
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 21%retrieval 83%

KEYWORDS: microfluidic reactor, hydroxymethyl phosphonates, continuous synthesis, phosphite esters, formaldehyde, flow chemistry, high yield, high purity, acid number, green chemistry, optimization, dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate, diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate, mass transfer, heat transfer.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

10Oxygen-Bridged Hybrid Metallocene−Nonmetallocene Polymetallic Catalysts of Group 4 Metals for Bimodal Activity in Olefin Polymerization: Synthesis, Characterization, and Theoretical Investigation†
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 18%retrieval 92%
Keywords/terms: Oxygen-bridged, metallocene, nonmetallocene, polymetallic catalysts, Group 4 metals, bimodal activity, olefin polymerization, synthesis, characterization, DFT calculations.

This 2007 article reports the synthesis, characterization, and theoretical investigation of a new class of oxygen-bridged hybrid metallocene-nonmetallocene catalysts using Group 4 metals. The objective was to develop catalysts with bimodal activity in olefin polymerization. The study synthesized heterobimetallic and heterotrimetallic complexes, specifically Cp*2(Me)Zr(µ-O)Ti(NMe2)3 (7) and Cp*2(Me)Zr(µ-O)Hf(NMe2)2(µ-O)Zr(Me)Cp*2 (9), and characterized them using NMR spectroscopy, EI mass spectrometry, and single-crystal X-ray diffraction. The key finding is that complex 7 exhibits bimodal activity when activated with methylalumoxane (MAO), producing polyethylene primarily by the zirconium center and polystyrene by the titanium center. DFT calculations support these findings, suggesting that the titanium-centered cation is sterically more accessible for monomer binding, though energetically less favorable compared to the zirconium-centered cation. This work highlights the potential of polymetallic catalysts for tailored polymerization behavior, offering an advancement over single-metal catalysts.

KEYWORDS: antimicrobial resistance, oligohexamethylene guanidine, bihydrocarbonate, microfluidic synthesis, flow-type reactor, 13C NMR spectroscopy, HPLC, polycondensation, hexamethylenediamine, guanidine hydrochloride, process optimization, chemical purity, alkylguanidine.

BODY: Objective: To develop a microfluidic synthesis method for oligohexamethylene guanidine bihydrocarbonate (OHMG-BHC) in a flow-type reactor, evaluate its efficiency compared to classical bulk synthesis, and assess the purity of the resulting products. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. The structural integrity and purity of the products were analyzed using 13C NMR spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Results: 13C NMR analysis revealed that the microfluidic method successfully yielded a branched oligomeric structure with fewer unidentifiable impurities compared to bulk synthesis. HPLC analysis showed that the microfluidic approach resulted in a 1.5-fold lower concentration of unreacted initial monomers (hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate). Novelty: This study demonstrates the advantages of utilizing continuous-flow microfluidic hardware over traditional bulk reactors to streamline the synthesis of OHMG derivatives while significantly enhancing chemical purity and reaction completeness.

BODY: This paper investigates the formation of poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) microparticles and capsules via the selective extraction of aqueous polymer solution droplets generated using microfluidics and immersed in a non-solvent bath. Using a flow-focusing geometry, monodisperse droplets were produced in a hexadecane carrier phase and extracted into ethyl acetate. A descriptive model was applied to parameterize droplet shrinkage and extraction kinetics. The novelty lies in establishing comprehensive design criteria for PVA particles and capsules, linking thermodynamic and hydrodynamic factors to final morphology.

Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. Novelty: This study demonstrates the advantages of utilizing continuous-flow microfluidic hardware over traditional bulk reactors to streamline the synthesis of OHMG derivatives while significantly enhancing chemical purity and reaction completeness.

BODY: This review article explores the recent advancements and applications of microfluidic paper-based analytical extraction devices (µPAEDs) as a cost-effective, portable, and decentralized solution for detecting biomarkers, chemical contaminants, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Conventional extraction methods coupled with high-end chromatography (such as LC-MS/MS and GC-MS/MS) are often expensive, slow, require centralized facilities, and use environmentally harmful reagents. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed all-in-one µPAEDs that integrate sample extraction and detection onto a single paper-based platform. The article highlights the classification and detection of various analytes across diverse sample types—including blood, urine, saliva, sweat, interstitial fluid, food, water, and breath. Furthermore, it details the integration of technologies like molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs), ion-imprinted polymers (IIPs), digital image colorimetry (DIC), and electrochemical sensing. The novelty of this review lies in its comprehensive compilation of recent innovations in µPAEDs, emphasizing both invasive and non-invasive testing (such as VOC breath analysis) and outlining future perspectives toward smart, wearable diagnostic tools.

BODY: This paper presents the development and implementation of a hybrid microfluidic chip and tube system integrated with fluorescent molecularly imprinted polymer (MIP) core-shell particles for the extraction, derivatisation, and selective detection of peptides with N-terminating phosphorylated tyrosine (pY). The primary objective is to overcome limitations in detecting low-abundant phosphorylated peptides in complex bioanalytical samples, which are crucial biomarkers for early cancer diagnosis and neurodegenerative disorders. The methodology combines a modular tube-based reaction unit for N-terminus Fmoc derivatisation and ion exchange with a multi-layered PDMS/Teflon/glass microfluidic chip. This chip utilizes micropillar-stabilized parallel-flow micro-extractors for reagent cleanup (removing excess Fmoc-Cl with hexane) and selective analyte phase-transfer into an organic phase (chloroform) containing the M1 MIP sensory particles. A miniaturized opto-electronic read-out assembly utilizing an LED, optical fibers, and a USB spectrometer measures the "light-up" fluorescence response (LE and ESPT emission bands) in real time. The results demonstrate the successful discrimination of pY-terminating oligopeptides from their non-phosphorylated counterparts with a dynamic range of 1.5–50 \u03bcM and a total analysis time of 20 minutes per sample. The novelty lies in translating bead-based MIP ratiometric fluorescence sensing into a fully integrated, automated, continuous microfluidic platform capable of handling liquid-liquid extractions and specific phosphopeptide recognition without relying on costly antibodies.

5Understanding the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder reactions

Keywords/terms: Diels–Alder reactions, activation energy, charge transfer, polar mechanism, electrophilicity, nucleophilicity.

The study investigates the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the correlation between activation energy and the polar character of the transition state structure. The research uses computational methods to analyze the electronic properties of DA reactions between cyclopentadiene and a series of substituted ethylenes. The objective is to emphasize the significant correlation between activation barriers and the polar character of transition states. The methodology involves DFT calculations to determine energies, geometries, and charge transfer (CT) at the transition states (TSs). Results indicate a strong relationship between CT at the TS and the reaction rate and showed that the synchronicity of the bond-formation process cannot be related with reaction rate. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar, polar, and ionic categories based on the CT. The novelty of the work lies in emphasizing the role of the polar character, as measured by CT, in controlling reaction rates and provides a framework to predict the feasibility of DA reactions based on the electrophilic/nucleophilic character of the reagents.

The study's objective was to determine how the physicochemical properties, specifically surface facets determining surface energy, influence enzyme-like activities. The methodology involved synthesizing Pd nanocrystals with {111} and {100} facets, using electron spin resonance spectroscopy to evaluate catalase and superoxide dismutase-like activities. The main finding reveals that lower surface energy {111}-faceted Pd octahedrons exhibit greater antioxidant enzyme-like activity than higher surface energy {100}-faceted Pd nanocubes. The octahedrons protected cells against oxidative stress better, suppressing reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and subsequently protecting biomolecules and cell organelles. Results also demonstrate the role of surface facets in antioxidant enzyme mimics.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.
