BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

The study investigates the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the correlation between activation energy and the polar character of the transition state structure. The research uses computational methods to analyze the electronic properties of DA reactions between cyclopentadiene and a series of substituted ethylenes. The objective is to emphasize the significant correlation between activation barriers and the polar character of transition states. The methodology involves DFT calculations to determine energies, geometries, and charge transfer (CT) at the transition states (TSs). Results indicate a strong relationship between CT at the TS and the reaction rate and showed that the synchronicity of the bond-formation process cannot be related with reaction rate. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar, polar, and ionic categories based on the CT. The novelty of the work lies in emphasizing the role of the polar character, as measured by CT, in controlling reaction rates and provides a framework to predict the feasibility of DA reactions based on the electrophilic/nucleophilic character of the reagents.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This study investigates the role of component interactions at solid/liquid and liquid/liquid interfaces during oil-in-water (o/w) emulsification using microfluidic EDGE devices. The objective is to understand how these interactions affect droplet formation behaviour and operational pressure stability. Using various oil and emulsifier combinations—including alkanes, vegetable oils, surfactants, and proteins—the authors demonstrate that surfactants with strong glass interactions (e.g., Tween 20) facilitate stable emulsification, whereas weakly interacting surfactants can be displaced by strongly interacting triglycerides found in vegetable oil, leading to failure in producing monodisperse droplets. Proteins (such as WPI, alpha-lactalbumin, beta-lactalbumin, and BSA) form robust, hydrophilic films on solid surfaces that resist oil displacement, yielding significantly higher pressure stabilities and droplet formation frequencies compared to conventional surfactants. The novelty lies in establishing guidelines that view construction material, product formulations, and throughput as an integrated package rather than isolated aspects. This study, published in 2024, investigates molecular adsorption on graphene-supported platinum (Pt) subnanoclusters using density functional theory (DFT) calculations with D3 corrections. The objective was to understand the adsorption mechanisms of CO, NO, N2, and O2 on Pt subnanoclusters and their catalytic potential, comparing gas-phase and graphene-supported scenarios. The methodology involved DFT calculations to characterize the adsorption of the mentioned molecules on Pt subnanoclusters (Pt3 and Pt6). The main findings reveal that stronger interactions occur on the smaller Pt3 subnanoclusters or with specific molecules such as CO and NO. Conversely, Pt6 demonstrated greater stability and was better suited for O2 adsorption, with molecular dissociation observed. The study emphasizes the significant role of the graphene substrate in enhancing stability. The novelty lies in a detailed analysis of the electronic structure and charge transfer mechanisms involved in molecular adsorption on supported subnanoclusters, providing insights into catalytic optimization.

9Understanding the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder reactions
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 4%retrieval 93%
Keywords/terms: Diels–Alder reactions, activation energy, charge transfer, polar mechanism, electrophilicity, nucleophilicity.

The study investigates the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the correlation between activation energy and the polar character of the transition state structure. The research uses computational methods to analyze the electronic properties of DA reactions between cyclopentadiene and a series of substituted ethylenes. The objective is to emphasize the significant correlation between activation barriers and the polar character of transition states. The methodology involves DFT calculations to determine energies, geometries, and charge transfer (CT) at the transition states (TSs). Results indicate a strong relationship between CT at the TS and the reaction rate and showed that the synchronicity of the bond-formation process cannot be related with reaction rate. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar, polar, and ionic categories based on the CT. The novelty of the work lies in emphasizing the role of the polar character, as measured by CT, in controlling reaction rates and provides a framework to predict the feasibility of DA reactions based on the electrophilic/nucleophilic character of the reagents.

This study, titled "Intercalation-Activated Layered MoO3 Nanobelts as Biodegradable Nanozymes for Tumor-Specific Photo-Enhanced Catalytic Therapy," published in 2022, investigates the activation of layered MoO3 nanobelts via Na+/H2O co-intercalation to create a biodegradable nanozyme for tumor-specific photo-enhanced catalytic therapy. The methodology involved grinding long MoO3 nanobelts, intercalating them with Na+ and H2O to form NH MoO3x nanobelts, and modifying them with bovine serum albumin (BSA). The results indicated that these modified nanobelts exhibit excellent enzyme-mimicking catalytic activity, particularly for generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). The photothermal effect under 1064 nm laser irradiation further enhanced this activity, leading to effective in vitro cancer cell-killing and in vivo tumor elimination. The novelty lies in employing intercalation to activate layered MoO3 for biomedical applications, showing enhanced performance compared to the native MoO3 nanobelts.

This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. Results indicated that DESs, particularly ChCl/xylitol and ChCl/1,2-propanediol, showed good solubility for phenolic compounds. This work distinguishes itself by being the first to extract phenolic compounds from VOO using DESs, proposing a more efficient, safer, sustainable, and cost-effective alternative to methanol.

Objective: To develop a general and efficient method for the deoxygenative amination of activated alcohols, particularly those with challenging substituents like trifluoromethyl groups. Methodology: The study employed an electrochemical paired electrolysis approach using alcohol-derived carbazates and nitrobenzene. Various primary, secondary, and tertiary alkylamines were synthesized. Optimization of reaction conditions was performed to maximize yields. Mechanistic studies included radical trapping experiments, investigation of reaction intermediates, and cyclic voltammetry. Results: A general electrochemical paired electrolysis method was developed for synthesizing primary, secondary, and tertiary amines from functionalized alcohols, including those with α-CF3, α-CF2H, and benzyl substituents. The method utilized carbazates and nitroarenes. The practicality of the method was demonstrated using electrochemical continuous flow technique, and a plausible reaction mechanism was proposed, with yields ranging from 38-74%. The findings highlight the successful harnessing of stabilized and activated radicals for further derivatization which differed from prior studies.

BODY: This study investigates the in situ formation of leak-free polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogel membranes in microfluidic fuel cells to address the persistent problem of fuel crossover under co-laminar flows. The objective was to create a membrane that prevents the mixing of incompatible electrolytes (acid and base) while selectively controlling molecular diffusion. Utilizing a blended ratio of PEG monomers (Mn250 and Mn575 in an 8:2 ratio), the researchers successfully eliminated membrane swelling and deformation issues while providing sufficient ionic conductivity and selective permeability. A finite difference transport model was implemented to simulate glucose diffusion profiles within the microfluidic channel. Results demonstrate that the optimized PEG membrane completely blocks larger molecules like trypan blue and significantly retards glucose diffusion. By combining the leak-free PEG membrane with an optimal continuous flow rate of 20 ΓΔ min−1, the microfluidic fuel cell successfully prevents fuel crossover, rapidly flushes diffused glucose from the cathode compartment, and generates an open circuit voltage (OCV) of up to ~450 mV from 10 mM of glucose. The novelty lies in the successful in situ photopolymerization of a tunable, non-swelling PEG membrane inside a microfluidic device operating with incompatible electrolytes.

BODY: This paper presents a novel microfluidic approach for the generation and active control of stable, monodisperse oil-in-water droplets in the ultralow interfacial tension (ULIFT) regime (0.1–1 mN m⁻¹). The objective is to overcome the challenge of extremely slow capillary breakup times and shear-driven polydispersity that typically hinder droplet formation at very low surface tensions. The methodology utilizes a tunable oil-water-surfactant system comprising heptane, water, sodium chloride, and the surfactant aerosol OT (AOT). By integrating an on-chip temperature control unit and controlling the emulsion salinity via Y-junction mixing, the equilibrium surface tension is actively managed within a flow-focusing junction (FFJ) and a separate observation chamber (ObC). Results demonstrate that while direct formation at ultralow tension leads to droplet rupture due to viscous stresses, raising the temperature locally increases the surface tension just enough to allow smooth droplet generation (coefficients of variation under 3.5%). Subsequent storage near the microemulsion phase transition successfully induces observable thermal capillary waves (root-mean-square displacement around 110 nm), confirming the ultralow interfacial tension regime. The novelty lies in the decoupled active control of salinity and temperature within a microfluidic platform, enabling both stable monodisperse droplet production and subsequent real-space investigation of thermal capillary phenomena without external mechanical vibration. The study investigates the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the correlation between activation energy and the polar character of the transition state structure. The research uses computational methods to analyze the electronic properties of DA reactions between cyclopentadiene and a series of substituted ethylenes. The objective is to emphasize the significant correlation between activation barriers and the polar character of transition states. The methodology involves DFT calculations to determine energies, geometries, and charge transfer (CT) at the transition states (TSs). Results indicate a strong relationship between CT at the TS and the reaction rate and showed that the synchronicity of the bond-formation process cannot be related with reaction rate. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar, polar, and ionic categories based on the CT. The novelty of the work lies in emphasizing the role of the polar character, as measured by CT, in controlling reaction rates and provides a framework to predict the feasibility of DA reactions based on the electrophilic/nucleophilic character of the reagents.

BODY: This study investigates pore-scale membrane fouling mechanisms using a microfluidic membrane mimic (MMM) system featuring a staggered arrangement of pillars with a 2 m gap, replicating microfiltration pore sizes. Conducted under constant-pressure dead-end filtration, the research examines fouling dynamics using three synthetic wastewater foulants: polystyrene (PS) particle solutions, polyacrylamide (PAM) polymer solutions, and their mixtures. The results reveal four major microscopic fouling categories: upstream cake filtration, pore blocking, downstream colloidal aggregation, and downstream colloidal streamer fouling. At lower pressures, cake filtration and pore blocking dominate due to attractive electrostatic interactions, whereas higher pressures and shear rates induce significant downstream colloidal aggregation and filamentous streamer formation, leading to severe flux decline in combined fouling scenarios. Reversibility tests indicate that colloidal aggregation is largely reversible via hydraulic washing, whereas colloidal streamer fouling is predominantly irreversible. Hermia model analysis suggests that fouling behavior aligns closely with complete pore blocking signatures. Novelty lies in the real-time in-situ pore-scale visualization and characterization of previously understudied downstream phenomena and abiotic colloidal streamers. BODY: This paper introduces a chemically patterned microfluidic paper-based analytical device (C-uPAD) designed for point-of-care (POC) diagnostics and environmental monitoring. The objective was to overcome the limitations of traditional microfluidic paper-based analytical device (uPAD) fabrication methods—such as instability under high temperatures and sensitivity to organic solvents—by creating thermally and chemically stable hydrophobic barriers. The methodology involves using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of trichlorosilane (TCS) onto chromatography paper to form covalent bonds with hydroxyl groups on cellulose fibers. The C-uPAD platform was validated through three applications: a glucose assay (achieving a limit of detection (LOD) of 13 mg/dL for well-spot and 23 mg/dL for lateral flow), a tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa) sandwich immunoassay (achieving an LOD of 3 ng/mL), and heavy metal detection of nickel (Ni) using dimethylglyoxime (DMG) coupled via thermal condensation of APTES (achieving an LOD of 150 ug/L). BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This critical review examines the microfluidic synthesis of radiotracers for positron emission tomography (PET) and explores prospects for commercialization and decentralized dose-on-demand production. Currently, clinical PET is dominated by [18F]FDG due to the high costs associated with centralized high-volume manufacturing infrastructure, which makes the production of alternative boutique radiotracers economically unviable. Microfluidic technologies offer a solution by utilizing lower reagent volumes, enhancing mass and heat transfer, and accelerating reaction rates. The review categorizes microfluidic radiotracer production systems into continuous flow, batch, and droplet approaches, detailing early research, recent advancements, and highly integrated platforms such as Advion Nanotek, ISAR, iMiDEV, and droplet-screening instruments. Furthermore, critical financial, safety, and regulatory considerations—including shielding, automation, material compatibility (e.g., PDMS vs. COP/COC and PEEK), activity tracking, and quality control developments like Tracer-QC and QC1—are analyzed to determine what is necessary to transition these platforms from academic laboratories to commercial, benchtop clinical settings. BODY: This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a continuous-flow, well-mixed multi-well microfluidic device for the parallel screening of crystal polymorphs, morphology, and growth rates at controlled supersaturation. The primary objective is to overcome the limitations of traditional microtiter plates and single-stream microfluidic setups, which suffer from solute depletion, varying downstream compositions, and inaccurate crystallization kinetics. The methodology introduces a merged-inlet configuration using Y-junctions with vertical offsets to consolidate alternate tangential inlets of cyclonic micromixers into an array of eight wells, thereby reducing the number of required external pumps while maintaining identical pressure drops and uniform mixing. Computational fluid dynamics simulations were performed using COMSOL Multiphysics to verify velocity, pressure, and concentration profiles, alongside residence time distribution analysis. The device was experimentally benchmarked using ortho-aminobenzoic acid (o-ABA) and subsequently applied to screen L-histidine via antisolvent crystallization across eight different solution conditions (varying molar concentrations, ethanol volume percentages, and supersaturations) over a 30-minute duration. Results demonstrate that the multi-well microfluidic device successfully captures both stable and metastable polymorphs and extracts reliable crystal growth rates without supersaturation depletion. Conversely, conventional 96-well microtiter plates overestimate the fraction of stable polymorphs due to Ostwald ripening and introduce high uncertainties in growth rate measurements. The novelty lies in the first-time integration of parallel-connected, multi-inlet cyclonic micromixers for high-throughput, steady-state continuous-flow crystallization screening.

The novelty lies in establishing comprehensive design criteria for PVA particles and capsules, linking thermodynamic and hydrodynamic factors to final morphology.

1Acid-mediated reactions under microfluidic conditions: A new strategy for practical synthesis of biofunctional natural products

KEYWORDS: [microfluidic conditions, acid-mediated reactions, natural products synthesis, oligosaccharides, pristane, glycosylation, reductive opening, benzylidene acetal, dehydration, micromixing, continuous flow microreactor, N-glycans, stereoselective synthesis]

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This mini-review introduces microfluidic plasma as a novel process intensification strategy that integrates microfluidic systems with plasma technology, leveraging their synergistic advantages for chemistry and chemical engineering. The methodology categorizes microfluidic plasmas into three primary configurations based on reactor design: chip-based, tubular-based, and jet-based microfluidic plasmas. The results demonstrate the broad utility and high efficiency of these systems across diverse applications, including the continuous synthesis of ligand-free gold nanoparticles and carbon dots, enhanced chemical synthesis (such as cyclohexane amination and hydrogen peroxide production), water treatment (organic pollutant degradation and biofilm removal), and surface/biomedical modifications. BODY: Objective: To determine the kinetic association rate constants and investigate the feasibility of continuous microfluidic synthesis for radiopharmaceuticals, specifically focusing on [177Lu]Lu-DOTA-TATE production. Methodology: A microfluidic setup featuring capillary tubing and heating blocks coupled with offline UHPLC analysis was utilized to evaluate reaction kinetics across various temperatures and capillary diameters. Computational simulations using COMSOL Multiphysics and the Finite Element Method modeled fluid flow, mass transfer, and heat transfer. Results: The reaction achieved a 99% yield at 80 °C within 44 s in a 100 µm microfluidic channel. Arrhenius parameters (A = 1.24 x 10^19 M^-1 s^-1, E_A = 109.5 kJ mol^-1) were determined for the first time. Simulations demonstrated that increasing the reactor diameter above 500 µm allows clinical-scale volumes (3 mL) to be processed in under 12 minutes. Novelty: This study provides the first experimentally derived kinetic rate constants and Arrhenius parameters for the Lu-DOTA-TATE conjugate, demonstrating that continuous microfluidic systems are viable alternatives to conventional batch-wise radiolabelling. Using a Si-bonded glass microfluidic device, metal nitrate solutions and sodium carbonate were co-precipitated under controlled conditions. The characterization employed X-ray diffraction (XRD), physisorption (BET), N2O pulse chemisorption, H2-TPR, in situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with EDX mapping. In catalytic activity tests at 250 °C with CO/CO2 feeds, the microfluidically prepared catalyst achieved superior methanol productivity, though it also produced dimethyl ether as a byproduct due to increased active surface acidity. The novelty lies in scaling up microfluidic co-precipitation for structured Cu-based catalysts and highlighting its benefits for uniform phase nucleation and improved catalytic performance. Chemical EngineeringPhysical Sciencesrerank 26%retrieval 83%

The article, published in 2019, introduces a novel sandwiched liquid-membrane electrodialysis system for selective lithium extraction from salt lake brines with a high Mg/Li ratio. The objective was to address the challenge of separating lithium from magnesium in brines, which represents a significant hurdle in lithium extraction. The methodology involved using a sandwiched liquid membrane composed of two cation exchange membranes and a Li+-loaded organic liquid film. The TBP+ClO4 system was selected as the optimal liquid film. The results demonstrated that the Mg/Li ratio in the catholyte was reduced to less than 2 from an initial ratio of 100 in the brine, with a specific energy consumption as low as 0.13 kWh·mol-1 Li. The optimal voltage and temperature were determined to be 3.00 V and 20°C, respectively. The system showed strong adaptability to brines with different cation compositions, effectively separating Li+ from other impurity cations like Na+, K+, Mg2+, and Ca2+. The novelty lies in the combination of liquid membrane extraction and electrodialysis, offering a promising approach for lithium extraction from brines with a high Mg/Li ratio, demonstrating high selectivity, low energy consumption, and environmental friendliness.

Требуется предложить антиоксидант для углеводородной смазочной композиции, в структуре которого одновременно присутствуют фенольная гидроксильная группа и аминный фрагмент, способные работать как взаимодополняющие центры торможения радикального окисления. Желательно, чтобы соединение растворялось в базовом масле не хуже чем на уровне 1–3 мас.% без визуального расслоения, не выпадало в осадок при хранении и не ухудшало внешний вид композиции. Лабораторный образец должен быть получен массой не менее 1 г, ориентир по чистоте — не ниже 90–95 %, с подтверждением структуры и оценкой профиля примесей. Предпочтительны молекулы с гидрофобным фрагментом примерно C8–C18, поскольку слишком полярные структуры могут хуже совмещаться с масляной средой, а слишком низкомолекулярные — быть менее технологичными как присадки. Предельная себестоимость пока не задана, но нужно оценить стоимость сырья в руб./г и руб./кг продукта, сравнить несколько маршрутов и не выбирать вариант только по максимальной активности, если он требует дефицитных реагентов или плохо масштабируется.

The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

BODY: This paper presents a simple and low-cost method to enhance fluorescence and luminescence signal intensities in poly(dimethyl) siloxane (PDMS)-based microfluidic devices by modifying the optical properties of the polymer. The approach involves suspending titanium dioxide (TiO2) particles within the PDMS to create an opaque, white composite material with high light-reflection properties. The methodology includes fabricating microfluidic chips using standard soft lithography by mixing sieved TiO2 powder into PDMS prepolymer at various concentrations (up to 21.4% w/w), curing, and bonding to glass coverslips. The results demonstrate that the TiO2-PDMS composite increases collected fluorescence signals by up to 11-fold for green- and red-emitting fluorophores and improves luminescence assays by enhancing back-reflection and reducing ambient background light. The novelty lies in integrating a high-refractive-index white pigment directly into standard PDMS microfluidic fabrication to achieve significant sensitivity gains without requiring complex optical setups.

BODY: This paper introduces a chemically patterned microfluidic paper-based analytical device (C-uPAD) designed for point-of-care (POC) diagnostics and environmental monitoring. The objective was to overcome the limitations of traditional microfluidic paper-based analytical device (uPAD) fabrication methods—such as instability under high temperatures and sensitivity to organic solvents—by creating thermally and chemically stable hydrophobic barriers. The methodology involves using chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of trichlorosilane (TCS) onto chromatography paper to form covalent bonds with hydroxyl groups on cellulose fibers. Optimal conditions were determined by controlling temperature, pattern size, and CVD duration (specifically 30 seconds at 53 degrees Celsius). The C-uPAD platform was validated through three applications: a glucose assay (achieving a limit of detection (LOD) of 13 mg/dL for well-spot and 23 mg/dL for lateral flow), a tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa) sandwich immunoassay (achieving an LOD of 3 ng/mL), and heavy metal detection of nickel (Ni) using dimethylglyoxime (DMG) coupled via thermal condensation of APTES (achieving an LOD of 150 ug/L). The novelty lies in the single-step, rapid, and solvent-resistant fabrication process utilizing CVD silanization and thermal condensation coupling, which provides high stability, adaptability, and clinically relevant LODs without requiring complex laboratory equipment.

This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The objective was to develop a sensitive and selective method for detecting antioxidants using a MnO2/Graphene Quantum Dot (GQD) composite with oxidase-like activity. The methodology involved synthesizing the composite via a hydrothermal method and using it as a nanozyme to catalyze the oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB), quantified by color changes. The results showed the developed assay achieved high selectivity and sensitivity for gallic acid, tannic acid, and ascorbic acid, with detection limits of 0.07, 0.28, and 0.69 μmol L−1, respectively. The sensor accurately measured and discriminated antioxidants in real food samples, demonstrating its potential for rapid food analysis. This work distinguishes itself by its use of an oxidase-like nanozyme, which eliminates the need for hydrogen peroxide, providing a simpler and more stable sensing system compared to peroxidase-mimicking nanozymes.

KEYWORDS: Oil Films; Gas-Assisted Gravity Drainage; Microfluidics; Norland Optic Adhesives-81; Enhanced Oil Recovery; Spreading Coefficient; Three-Phase Flow; Reservoir Porous Media; Interfacial Tension; Decane; Soltrol; Pore Network Geometry; Statistical Analysis; Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon Test; Wetting Characteristics BODY: The objective of this study was to visualize and evaluate the formation, stability, and thickness of oil films during three-phase flow (oil, water, and gas) in porous media, specifically simulating the Gas-Assisted Gravity Drainage (GAGD) enhanced oil recovery process. The methodology employed a novel transparent microfluidic platform fabricated using Norland Optic Adhesives-81 (NOA81) featuring a randomized pore network geometry designed to mimic consolidated water-wet sandstone reservoirs with channel widths varying from 15 to 50 micrometers. Experiments were conducted using positive (Soltrol-water-air) and negative (decane-water-air) oil spreading systems mounted vertically on an inverted microscope. The results demonstrated that continuous, significantly thinner oil films formed in the positive spreading system, whereas discontinuous, trapped oil droplets were predominantly encountered in the negative spreading system. Statistical analysis using the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test confirmed a significant difference in dimensionless oil phase thicknesses between the two systems (P-value = 0.0029). The novelty of this work lies in the utilization of the chemically and physically resistant NOA81 microfluidic platform with realistic pore geometries to directly visualize and quantify microscale three-phase flow mechanisms and fluid distributions previously only inferred in conventional corefloods. 9Acid-mediated reactions under microfluidic conditions: A new strategy for practical synthesis of biofunctional natural products
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 4%retrieval 92%

KEYWORDS: [microfluidic conditions, acid-mediated reactions, natural products synthesis, oligosaccharides, pristane, glycosylation, reductive opening, benzylidene acetal, dehydration, micromixing, continuous flow microreactor, N-glycans, stereoselective synthesis]

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

Proteins (such as WPI, alpha-lactalbumin, beta-lactalbumin, and BSA) form robust, hydrophilic films on solid surfaces that resist oil displacement, yielding significantly higher pressure stabilities and droplet formation frequencies compared to conventional surfactants. The novelty lies in establishing guidelines that view construction material, product formulations, and throughput as an integrated package rather than isolated aspects. BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The article describes the synthesis and characterization of tetranitro-, tetraamino-, and tetra(4-pyridylimino)tetrahydroxythiacalix[4]arene derivatives. The objective was to explore the nitration of tetrahydroxythiacalix[4]arene, a process poorly documented compared to its calixarene counterparts, and to synthesize related amino and imino derivatives. The methodology involved nitration using a novel procedure with nitrosium nitrate complexes, followed by reduction to amino derivatives via Sn/HCl and subsequent reactions with pyridine-4-carboxyaldehyde. The study found that the nitration reaction was highly influenced by the solvent. The resulting tetranitro derivative was characterized using various spectroscopic techniques and X-ray diffraction, revealing its 1,2-alternate conformation. Thermal analysis of the synthesized compounds was also performed. The novelty lies in the successful nitration of thiacalix[4]arene using nitrosium nitrate and the subsequent derivatization, which contrasts with the failures of previously reported methods and lack of prior literature on this topic. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. The structural integrity and purity of the products were analyzed using 13C NMR spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). BODY: This paper presents a novel continuous synthesis method for hydroxymethyl phosphonates (HPs) using a microfluidic reactor to address the limitations of conventional organic synthesis, which typically suffers from strong heat-release, high by-product formation, elevated acid numbers, and low yields. The objective was to design a controlled flow system utilizing phosphite esters and formaldehyde as starting materials in the presence of triethylamine catalyst. The methodology involves a microfluidic reactor setup consisting of analytical liquid chromatography pumps, micro-mixers, a tubular micro-reactor, a back pressure valve, a heat exchanger, and a liquid-liquid separator for continuous phase separation. Process parameters such as molar ratio, reaction temperature, and residence time were systematically optimized for five different HPs: dimethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DMHP), diethyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DEHP), dipropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DPHP), diisopropyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DIHP), and dibutyl hydroxymethyl phosphonate (DBHP). The results demonstrate that the microfluidic approach successfully yields all targeted HPs exceeding 94% yield (94.2%-96.7%), purities above 99% (99.0%-99.3%), low water content (<0.08 wt%), and low acid numbers (<0.15 mg KOH/g). The novelty lies in the first-time application of a microfluidic reactor for HP synthesis, overcoming traditional amplification and heat-transfer bottlenecks while providing a safe, clean, continuous, and easily scalable production process.

BODY: This study investigates the application of a serpentine microfluidic device to improve the liquid-liquid extraction (LLE) performance for separating calcium ions (Ca2+) using Dicyclohexano-18-crown-6 (DC18C6) as a ligand in an organic phase of n-butyl acetate and an aqueous phase containing picric acid and calcium chloride. The objective is to overcome the limitations of conventional large-scale extraction methods, such as high residence time, large spatial requirements, and settling units. Utilizing a parallel flow regime inside a microchannel with a high surface-to-volume ratio, the methodology incorporates Response Surface Methodology (RSM) combined with a Box-Behnken design (BBD) to model and optimize independent process variables including aquatic phase flow rate (Q), DC18C6 concentration (C), and pH. The results demonstrate that the proposed serpentine microfluidic system achieves a microfluidic extraction percentage of 24.59% at a residence time of 4.2 s and an extraction efficiency of up to 63.6% under optimized conditions (pH 6.34, DC18C6 concentration of 0.015 M, and flow rate of 20 µl/min). The novelty lies in the demonstrated superior extraction performance and efficiency of the serpentine microchannel compared to traditional methods and alternative microfluidic geometries reported in the literature.

7Acid-mediated reactions under microfluidic conditions: A new strategy for practical synthesis of biofunctional natural products
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 9%retrieval 94%

KEYWORDS: [microfluidic conditions, acid-mediated reactions, natural products synthesis, oligosaccharides, pristane, glycosylation, reductive opening, benzylidene acetal, dehydration, micromixing, continuous flow microreactor, N-glycans, stereoselective synthesis]

BODY: This paper reviews the application of microfluidic systems to key acid-mediated reactions—specifically glycosylation, the reductive opening of benzylidene acetal groups, and dehydration—as a practical strategy for synthesizing biofunctional natural products like N-glycans and the immunostimulating natural terpenoid pristane. Traditionally problematic in batch stirring due to scale-up limitations, these rapid reactions were successfully controlled using continuous flow microreactors. The objective was to overcome traditional scale-up limitations involving mixing efficiency, temperature control, and side-reactions. The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. Results demonstrate that vigorous and rapid micromixing with concentrated acids drastically improves yields and stereoselectivity, enabling multi-gram and industrial-scale syntheses (e.g., kilogram-scale production of pristane with >99% purity) without the formation of typical batch by-products. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The study's objective was to develop low-viscosity deep eutectic solvents (DESs) for effective 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE) absorption, investigating the absorption performance, separation mechanism, and industrial process simulation. The methodology involved synthesizing DESs with varying hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and acceptors (HBAs), measuring their physicochemical properties, saturated absorption capacity, and employing 1H NMR, FT-IR, and quantum chemical calculations to elucidate the absorption mechanism. The results revealed that 3,4-DMOET:ButA (1:2 molar ratio) was the optimal absorbent due to its high saturated absorption capacity (2746 mg/g at 20 °C) and low viscosity. The absorption was found to be a physical process, with HBA-DCE interaction primarily involving C-H···π and C-H···Cl, and HBD-DCE interaction dominated by C-H···O HB and vdW interactions. Process simulation confirmed DES's high DCE removal performance, suggesting the strategy's broader applicability for VOC absorption.

9Electrochemical deoxygenative amination of stabilized alkyl radicals from activated alcohols

Keywords/terms: Electrochemical deoxygenative amination, alkyl radicals, activated alcohols, carbazates, nitrobenzene, paired electrolysis, trifluoromethylated compounds, continuous flow.

Objective: To develop a general and efficient method for the deoxygenative amination of activated alcohols, particularly those with challenging substituents like trifluoromethyl groups. Methodology: The study employed an electrochemical paired electrolysis approach using alcohol-derived carbazates and nitrobenzene. Various primary, secondary, and tertiary alkylamines were synthesized. Optimization of reaction conditions was performed to maximize yields. Mechanistic studies included radical trapping experiments, investigation of reaction intermediates, and cyclic voltammetry. Results: A general electrochemical paired electrolysis method was developed for synthesizing primary, secondary, and tertiary amines from functionalized alcohols, including those with α-CF3, α-CF2H, and benzyl substituents. The method utilized carbazates and nitroarenes. The practicality of the method was demonstrated using electrochemical continuous flow technique, and a plausible reaction mechanism was proposed, with yields ranging from 38-74%. The findings highlight the successful harnessing of stabilized and activated radicals for further derivatization which differed from prior studies.

The study investigates lithium iodide (LiI) as a catalyst for the Michael addition of β-dicarbonyl compounds. The objective is to find improved conditions for C-C bond formation, specifically in the context of α,β-unsaturated aldehydes, where conventional methods face limitations. The methodology involves using catalytic amounts of LiI in refluxing dimethoxyethane (DME) to facilitate the conjugate addition of β-diesters, β-ketoesters, and linear/cyclic β-diketones to Michael acceptors such as α,β-unsaturated ketones and aldehydes. The results demonstrate that LiI is an efficient catalyst, leading to excellent yields in the formation of adducts. This methodology facilitates an improved one-pot synthesis of 5,6-disubstituted cyclohex-2-en-1-ones using α,β-unsaturated aldehydes, which are key intermediates in natural product synthesis. The novelty lies in the use of LiI and its applicability to unsaturated aldehydes, improving upon the limitations of previous base-catalyzed processes and phase-transfer catalysis.

Запрос 12. Результаты литературного поиска

Требуется объяснить, что может измениться в свойствах антиоксиданта, если объединить в одной молекуле пространственно затрудненный фенольный фрагмент и аминный фрагмент, а не использовать их как отдельные добавки. Интересует, может ли такая архитектура повысить эффективность торможения окисления за счет последовательного перехвата пероксильных радикалов, стабилизации феноксильного радикала и возможного регенерационного взаимодействия между фрагментами. Также нужно оценить, как такое объединение скажется на растворимости в углеводородной среде, летучести, склонности к окрашиванию, совместимости с другими компонентами масла и технологичности получения. Желательно отдельно рассмотреть случаи, когда аминный фрагмент является алифатическим, ароматическим или бензильным, потому что их электронные свойства и влияние на стабильность радикалов могут различаться. Количественные требования к активности пока не заданы, поэтому важно предложить критерии сравнения таких гибридных молекул с обычными фенольными антиоксидантами и определить, при каких условиях гибридная структура действительно имеет смысл.

This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. Methodology involved synthesizing complexes, exchanging chloride ligands with various groups (halides, alkyls, etc.), and characterizing solid-state structures. Results showed that PHENI* catalysts, particularly titanium-based, exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for ethylene polymerization when heterogenized on sMAO. The study found that catalyst structure affects activity and ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) formation, offering insights into ion pairing and ligand geometry. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

The article published in 2010, investigates the synthesis and catalytic activity of mono-, bis-, and tris(phenoxy)-titanium(IV) chlorides with different alkyl/aryl substituents (Me, iPr, tBu, and Ph). The objective was to understand how the ancillary ligand influences the catalytic performance in ethylene polymerization. Various complexes, including [Cp*Ti(2-R-PhO)nCl3n], were prepared and characterized. The study revealed that the phenyl series demonstrated significantly higher catalytic activity than the Me, iPr, and tBu series, with the bis(phenoxide) complex 2PhCl showing the highest activity. Alkylation reactions with trimethylaluminum (TMA), triisobutylaluminum (TIBA), and methylaluminoxane (MAO) were performed to identify active species. DFT calculations supported the experimental findings, suggesting [Cp*Ti(2-Ph-PhO)MeCl] as the active species. Furthermore, homopolymerization of ethylene was carried out with methylated complexes, and the activity was correlated with the generation of active sites. The research provides insights into the effect of ligand clustering on catalytic performance at high temperatures. Tables: Table 1. BODY: This paper presents a novel one-step microfluidic approach for the simultaneous production and surface functionalization of polymer microfibers and microparticles. The methodology utilizes a capillary-based microfluidic device with two miscible or immiscible co-flowing phases: a core phase containing poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) and a photoinitiator, and a sheath phase containing multi-thiol or multi-amine functional molecules. Upon UV irradiation at 365 nm, PEGDA undergoes rapid photopolymerization to form the core fiber while simultaneously engaging in interfacial coupling reactions (thiol-acrylate or amine-acrylate) with molecules in the sheath phase. Results demonstrate that the surface density of functional groups can be effectively modulated by adjusting the initial concentration of the reactive molecules, their functionality (number of thiol or amine groups), and the sheath fluid flow rate. Ellman's test, Kaiser test, EDS, and contact angle measurements confirmed successful surface modification. Furthermore, biological evaluations using RAW264.7 murine macrophages revealed that thiol-modified microfibers significantly enhance cell adhesion compared to unmodified or amine-modified counterparts, highlighting their strong potential for tissue engineering scaffolds. The novelty lies in eliminating multi-step post-production surface modification processes, thereby reducing production time and costs while providing precise spatial control over surface chemistry. This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The objective was to develop a sensitive and selective method for detecting antioxidants using a MnO2/Graphene Quantum Dot (GQD) composite with oxidase-like activity. The methodology involved synthesizing the composite via a hydrothermal method and using it as a nanozyme to catalyze the oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB), quantified by color changes. The results showed the developed assay achieved high selectivity and sensitivity for gallic acid, tannic acid, and ascorbic acid, with detection limits of 0.07, 0.28, and 0.69 μmol L−1, respectively. The sensor accurately measured and discriminated antioxidants in real food samples, demonstrating its potential for rapid food analysis. This work distinguishes itself by its use of an oxidase-like nanozyme, which eliminates the need for hydrogen peroxide, providing a simpler and more stable sensing system compared to peroxidase-mimicking nanozymes.

The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. Results indicated that DESs, particularly ChCl/xylitol and ChCl/1,2-propanediol, showed good solubility for phenolic compounds. Specifically, the study found an increase in extraction yields of oleacein and oleocanthal by 20–33% and 67.9–68.3%, respectively, compared to conventional methods. This work distinguishes itself by being the first to extract phenolic compounds from VOO using DESs, proposing a more efficient, safer, sustainable, and cost-effective alternative to methanol.

The methodology utilized continuous flow microreactors (such as IMM and Comet X-01 micromixers) combined with precise temperature control, high concentrations of acids (e.g., TMSOTf, BF3·OEt2, p-TsOH), and controlled residence times. The novelty lies in establishing that microfluidic systems can fundamentally alter and optimize fast acid-mediated reactions, providing a robust, scalable alternative to conventional batch processes for complex organic synthesis.

The methodology involves utilizing micro-reactors and miniaturized platforms (developed under the EU-funded BIOINTENSE project) to test reaction options with reduced reagent inventories and precious biocatalysts like omega-transaminases. The results highlight how dimensionless numbers (Reynolds, Péclet, Bond, and Damköhler numbers) govern microfluidic flow behaviors, enabling enhanced heat and mass transfer, laminar flow advantages, and in situ product removal (ISPR). The novelty lies in shifting from case-by-case trial-and-error approaches to a standardized, high-throughput microfluidic toolbox for integrated protein and process engineering. The study investigates the mechanism of polar Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the correlation between activation energy and the polar character of the transition state structure. The research uses computational methods to analyze the electronic properties of DA reactions between cyclopentadiene and a series of substituted ethylenes. The objective is to emphasize the significant correlation between activation barriers and the polar character of transition states. The methodology involves DFT calculations to determine energies, geometries, and charge transfer (CT) at the transition states (TSs). Results indicate a strong relationship between CT at the TS and the reaction rate and showed that the synchronicity of the bond-formation process cannot be related with reaction rate. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar, polar, and ionic categories based on the CT. The novelty of the work lies in emphasizing the role of the polar character, as measured by CT, in controlling reaction rates and provides a framework to predict the feasibility of DA reactions based on the electrophilic/nucleophilic character of the reagents.

This 2009 study investigates the mechanism of Diels–Alder (DA) reactions, focusing on the relationship between their polar character and reaction rates. The objective was to understand how the polarity, quantified by charge transfer at the transition state (TS), influences the activation energy of DA reactions. The methodology involved DFT calculations at the B3LYP/6-31G* level to analyze the energies, geometries, and electronic structures of TSs for DA reactions between cyclopentadiene (Cp) and various substituted ethylenes. The main finding is a strong correlation (R² = 0.89) between the charge transfer at the TS and the activation barriers, showing that increased polarity accelerates the reaction. The study classifies DA reactions into non-polar (N), polar (P), and ionic (I) based on their charge transfer characteristics, contrasting with prior studies that did not emphasize the relevance of the polar character in these reactions. This work emphasizes the importance of polarity of reactions in predicting and explaining DA reaction rates, where it controls the reaction rates to a greater extent than the asynchronicity of the forming bonds.

BODY: This study investigates the impact of a polymer gel on oil and water permeability using a transparent microfluidic device. The primary objective is to evaluate permeability damage caused by gel treatments in porous media, providing insights for enhanced oil recovery (EOR) applications. The methodology involves fabricating a microchip with 50 µm wide channels using a UV-curable polymer (NOA81) via replica molding from a silicon/PDMS master. Flood experiments were conducted by saturating the microchip with brine and light crude oil, followed by the injection of a 0.5 wt% hydrolyzed polyacrylamide (HPAM) polymer solution crosslinked with 0.05 wt% chromium (III) acetate hydroxide. The results demonstrate that the introduction of the polymer gel significantly reduces fluid permeability. Specifically, water permeability decreased by a factor of 106 at the shock front and 24 after pressure stabilization, while oil permeability was reduced by at least 40 times before a microchip leak occurred at 296 kPa. BODY: This review article explores the recent advancements and applications of microfluidic paper-based analytical extraction devices (µPAEDs) as a cost-effective, portable, and decentralized solution for detecting biomarkers, chemical contaminants, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Conventional extraction methods coupled with high-end chromatography (such as LC-MS/MS and GC-MS/MS) are often expensive, slow, require centralized facilities, and use environmentally harmful reagents. To overcome these limitations, researchers have developed all-in-one µPAEDs that integrate sample extraction and detection onto a single paper-based platform. 1How imperfect mixing and differential diffusion accelerate the rate of nonlinear reactions in microfluidic channels

KEYWORDS: microfluidics, nonlinear reaction, autocatalysis, clock reaction, differential diffusion, iodate-arsenous acid reaction, laminar flow, mixing efficiency, Taylor dispersion, microtiter plate, Dushman reaction, Roebuck reaction, spatial segregation, reaction kinetics, numerical simulation. BODY: This study investigates the paradoxical phenomenon where imperfect mixing and spatial segregation accelerate the rate of a nonlinear autocatalytic reaction in microfluidic channels. Using the iodate–arsenous acid clock reaction as a model system, the authors compare reaction progress under batch conditions (in microtiter plates with varying shaking times and rotational speeds) and continuous-flow laminar microfluidic devices (with and without mixing obstacles). Results demonstrate that enhanced mixing (via prolonged shaking or flow obstructions) surprisingly prolongs the induction period, thus slowing down the reaction. Conversely, segregated reactant streams in microfluidic channels exhibit accelerated reaction rates at moderate inducer concentrations. Through one-dimensional numerical simulations of a generic cubic autocatalysis reaction-diffusion system, the authors show that this acceleration is governed by the interplay between nonlinear reaction kinetics and differential diffusion, where the autocatalytic species diffuses slower than the substrate. This creates localized high-concentration zones near the interface of segregated reactants. The findings highlight the successful harnessing of stabilized and activated radicals for further derivatization which differed from prior studies.

10Evaluation of first-principles Hubbard and Hund corrected DFT for defect formation energies in non-magnetic transition metal oxides
Materials SciencePhysical Sciencesrerank 4%retrieval 91%
Keywords/terms: DFT+U+J, defect formation energies, transition metal oxides, ZrO2, HfO2, TiO2, Hubbard U, Hund's J.

Objective: The study investigates the accuracy of first-principles DFT+U+J techniques for calculating defect formation energies in non-magnetic transition metal oxides (TMOs), focusing on ZrO2, HfO2, and TiO2, and addresses the challenges associated with environment-dependent U and J values. Methodology: The research compares defect properties calculated using PBE, DFT+U+J, and literature results in ZrO2, HfO2, and TiO2. It explores three methods to address the environment-dependent U and J value problem, namely, the "differing potentials", "subtraction", and "averaging" methods. Defect formation energies and transition levels were calculated for oxygen vacancies. Structures were analyzed, and defect concentrations were predicted. Results: The study reveals that the naive DFT+U+J approach yields unphysical results for defect formation energies, but the proposed correction methods restore results aligning with literature values. The "differing potentials" and "averaging" methods show good agreement with literature values for ZrO2 and HfO2. In TiO2, DFT+U+J provides results that are closer to GW results than PBE. The transition levels match previously published data. The study underscores the importance of consistent application of Hubbard corrections in DFT+U calculations for reliable predictions, and the "differing potentials" method is recommended.

Требуется оценить, насколько рационально использовать не одну гибридную молекулу, а смесь фенольного антиоксиданта и аминного антиоксиданта в одной масляной композиции. Нужно понять, будет ли эффект такой смеси просто аддитивным или возможна синергия, при которой один компонент замедляет расходование другого либо стабилизирует промежуточные радикальные формы. Важно оценить не только антиокислительную активность, но и совместимость компонентов между собой, растворимость в углеводородной среде, риск потемнения, выпадения осадка и изменения свойств композиции при хранении. Желательно ориентироваться на приготовление лабораторной композиции объемом не менее 100 мл и проверку отсутствия расслоения в течение 24 часов как минимальный критерий совместимости. Предельная стоимость компонентов пока не задана, поэтому нужно сравнить экономическую и технологическую целесообразность смеси с вариантом синтеза единой молекулы, учитывая доступность сырья, простоту проверки и перспективу масштабирования.

This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. The objective is to harness unique physical environments—such as laminar flow, precise concentration gradients, enhanced mass and heat transfer, and large surface-to-volume ratios—to steer self-assembly pathways. The methodology involves utilizing continuous-flow, droplet-based, and digital microfluidic platforms to control reactant mixing, supersaturation, and reaction-diffusion processes. Results demonstrate the successful isolation of intermediate states, kinetically trapped crystals, unprecedented morphologies (e.g., hollow frames, nanowires, and amorphous nanoparticles), and the direct surface integration of functional materials like conductive polymers, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and covalent organic frameworks (COFs). The novelty lies in using top-down microfluidic forces to exert fine spatio-temporal control over bottom-up molecular aggregation, enabling the generation of advanced functional materials and supramolecular systems that are otherwise unattainable through conventional bulk flask-mixing techniques. This 2024 study investigates permethylindenyl-phenoxy (PHENI*) transition-metal chloride complexes for ethylene polymerization, expanding on previous work with indenyl PHENICS catalysts. The objective was to synthesize and characterize PHENI* complexes (1-7) with varying ancillary ligands and group four metals (Ti, Zr, Hf) and evaluate their structure-reactivity relationships. Methodology involved synthesizing complexes, exchanging chloride ligands with various groups (halides, alkyls, etc.), and characterizing solid-state structures. Results showed that PHENI* catalysts, particularly titanium-based, exhibited exceptional catalytic activity for ethylene polymerization when heterogenized on sMAO. The study found that catalyst structure affects activity and ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) formation, offering insights into ion pairing and ligand geometry. High-pressure experiments further confirmed high activities and molecular weights for UHMWPE. The work demonstrates PHENI * catalysts as among the most active for controlled UHMWPE synthesis.

2Extraction of phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil by deep eutectic solvent (DES)
ChemistryPhysical Sciencesrerank 21%retrieval 81%
Keywords/terms: Deep eutectic solvents, Extraction, Phenolic compounds, Oleacein, Oleocanthal, Virgin olive oil. The 2015 Food Chemistry article introduces deep eutectic solvents (DESs) as "green" solvents for extracting phenolic compounds from virgin olive oil (VOO). The objective was to compare the efficiency of DESs with traditional methanol extraction. The methodology involved using various DES combinations (choline chloride with sugars, alcohols, organic acids, and urea) and comparing their extraction yields with conventional 80% methanol/water. Results indicated that DESs, particularly ChCl/xylitol and ChCl/1,2-propanediol, showed good solubility for phenolic compounds. Specifically, the study found an increase in extraction yields of oleacein and oleocanthal by 20–33% and 67.9–68.3%, respectively, compared to conventional methods. This work distinguishes itself by being the first to extract phenolic compounds from VOO using DESs, proposing a more efficient, safer, sustainable, and cost-effective alternative to methanol.

The article, published in 2018, reports on the asymmetric Michael addition reactions catalyzed by iron N-heterocyclic carbene (FeNHC) complexes. The objective was to study the Michael addition reactions of cyclic b-oxo ester and a-methyl cyano ester substrates with activated olefins using FeNHC complexes. The methodology involved synthesizing {Cp[1-benzyl-3-alkyl-benzimidazol-2-ylidene]Fe(CO)2}I complexes, where alkyl = i-Pr and Et, and employing them as catalysts in the presence of L-proline under ambient conditions. The results showed that the cyclic b-oxo ester substrates yielded up to 68% with 18% enantioselectivities, while the a-methyl cyano ester substrates gave up to 82% yields with 8% enantioselectivities. The study's novelty lies in the use of FeNHC complexes in the asymmetric Michael addition, which has not been extensively explored, and the mechanism was proposed based on mass spectrometry results.

Traditional under-oil open microfluidic systems (UOMS) suffer from low visual contrast between substrates and chemically defined surface patterns, making sample manipulation and focal-plane-sensitive characterization difficult. To overcome this, the authors introduce a semi-transparent 100-nm silicon (Si) nanolayer over the substrate patterns via e-beam vapor deposition, which enhances visual contrast for both naked-eye and microscope observation, improves optical access for inverted and upright microscopes, and reduces interfering Raman background noise from the underlying glass. The chemical stability of V-UOMS was validated against strong acids (pH < 1), strong bases (pH > 12), and hydrocarbon solvents (ethanol and acetone). The system's utility was successfully demonstrated by monitoring a model gas-evolution reaction (Na2CO3 and H2SO4) using time-series Raman measurements, and a gas-liquid reaction involving CO2 capture (Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O -> 2NaHCO3) under various oil overlays (silicone oils, fluorinert FC-40, and mineral oil) to adjust gas permeation rates. The V-UOMS platform provides a robust, clog-free alternative to closed microfluidic channels for studying multi-phase chemical and biochemical processes. This study, published in 2022, presents a novel colorimetric sensor for detecting antioxidants in food samples. The objective was to develop a sensitive and selective method for detecting antioxidants using a MnO2/Graphene Quantum Dot (GQD) composite with oxidase-like activity. The methodology involved synthesizing the composite via a hydrothermal method and using it as a nanozyme to catalyze the oxidation of 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB), quantified by color changes. The results showed the developed assay achieved high selectivity and sensitivity for gallic acid, tannic acid, and ascorbic acid, with detection limits of 0.07, 0.28, and 0.69 μmol L−1, respectively. The sensor accurately measured and discriminated antioxidants in real food samples, demonstrating its potential for rapid food analysis. This work distinguishes itself by its use of an oxidase-like nanozyme, which eliminates the need for hydrogen peroxide, providing a simpler and more stable sensing system compared to peroxidase-mimicking nanozymes.

BODY: This study presents a cost-effective, portable, and smartphone-assisted 3D origami microfluidic paper-based analytical device (µPAD) modified with photochemically synthesized monolayer graphene/platinum (G/Pt) nanocatalysts for the multiplex colorimetric detection of dopamine and NADH. Imbalances in these biomarkers are critically linked to neurological and metabolic disorders such as Parkinson's disease, depression, and stroke. The G/Pt nanocatalysts were prepared via UV-assisted photochemical reduction using varying precursor concentrations (2.5 to 10 mM). The optimized 10 mM G/Pt catalyst significantly enhanced reaction rates (up to 18 times faster) and improved surface hydrophilicity and pore infiltration on the paper substrate. A dedicated Android application developed using Kotlin and OpenCV automated the quantitative reading of colorimetric signals from hue and saturation channels. The sensor demonstrated reliable limits of detection (0.56 mM for dopamine and 0.99 mM for NADH) with low mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE < 1%). This work introduces a scalable platform for point-of-care health monitoring and multiplex biomarker detection.

BODY: Objective: To develop a microfluidic synthesis method for oligohexamethylene guanidine bihydrocarbonate (OHMG-BHC) in a flow-type reactor, evaluate its efficiency compared to classical bulk synthesis, and assess the purity of the resulting products. Methodology: The synthesis of OHMG-BHC was performed via polycondensation of hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate using both a classical volumetric capacitive reactor and a microfluidic flow system with a syringe pump and capillary reactor. The structural integrity and purity of the products were analyzed using 13C NMR spectroscopy and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Results: 13C NMR analysis revealed that the microfluidic method successfully yielded a branched oligomeric structure with fewer unidentifiable impurities compared to bulk synthesis. HPLC analysis showed that the microfluidic approach resulted in a 1.5-fold lower concentration of unreacted initial monomers (hexamethylenediamine and guanidine hydrogencarbonate). Novelty: This study demonstrates the advantages of utilizing continuous-flow microfluidic hardware over traditional bulk reactors to streamline the synthesis of OHMG derivatives while significantly enhancing chemical purity and reaction completeness.
